[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "title": "Principles of Mathematical Modeling and Differential Equations",
    "scope": "Introduces the concept of differential equations as mathematical models connecting changing quantities with their rates of change. Explains the foundational criteria of a valid model: analytical tractability and observational fidelity, including the iterative cycle of model refinement. Covers the historical foundation by Newton (1687) and Leibniz (1676) along with basic derivative notation.",
    "key_points": [
      "A differential equation connects an unknown function to one or more of its derivatives.",
      "A mathematical model must balance mathematical solvability with predictive accuracy within required tolerances.",
      "Discrepancies with empirical data necessitate revising underlying physical assumptions rather than mathematical rules.",
      "Newton formulated mechanics using fluxions/derivatives (1687); Leibniz introduced the term differential equation (1676) and dy/dx notation."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "title": "Fundamental Applied Models: Falling Object, Population, and Cooling",
    "scope": "Derives the three introductory first-order ordinary differential equations from physical principles. Analyzes a falling mass under gravity and linear drag, the Malthusian exponential population model, and Newton's law of cooling. Focuses on the physical parameters, equation structures, exact solutions, and limiting behaviors such as terminal velocity.",
    "key_points": [
      "Falling object equation: m(dv/dt) = mg - kv or dv/dt = g - (k/m)v, yielding v(t) = mg/k + C exp(-kt/m) with terminal velocity v_max = mg/k.",
      "Malthusian population model: dN/dt = (alpha - beta)N = rN, leading to exponential trajectory N(t) = N_0 exp(r(t - t_0)) with unbounded growth for r > 0.",
      "Newton's law of cooling heat exchange: dQ = alpha*S*(T - T_a)dt matched with internal thermal energy dQ = c*rho*V*dT.",
      "Cooling ODE: dT/dt = -r(T - T_a) with lumped rate constant r = (alpha*S)/(c*rho*V) > 0."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 3,
    "title": "Classification by Type and Order",
    "scope": "Establishes formal classifications of differential equations based on independent variables and derivative orders. Distinguishes ordinary differential equations (single independent variable) from partial differential equations (multiple independent variables). Defines equation order via the highest derivative, contrasting the implicit n-th order form with explicit normal forms.",
    "key_points": [
      "Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) involve functions of one independent variable (e.g., RLC circuit: L d^2Q/dt^2 + R dQ/dt + Q/C = E(t)).",
      "Partial differential equations (PDEs) involve partial derivatives of functions of several variables (e.g., heat equation: du/dt = alpha d^2u/dx^2).",
      "The order of an equation is determined by its highest-order derivative.",
      "General implicit n-th order ODE form F(t, x, dx/dt, ..., d^n x/dt^n) = 0 versus explicit first-order normal form dx/dt = f(t, x).",
      "Duffing equation (x'' + kx + x^3 = B cos t) classified as a second-order equation."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 4,
    "title": "Systems of Differential Equations and Autonomous Systems",
    "scope": "Extends single differential equations to systems of coupled first-order ODEs. Formulates systems in normal scalar form and compact vector matrix notation. Defines autonomous systems by the absence of explicit independent variable dependence, illustrated through predator-prey dynamics and epidemic models.",
    "key_points": [
      "Scalar normal form for a system of n first-order equations: dx_i/dt = f_i(t, x_1, ..., x_n) for i = 1, ..., n.",
      "Vector formulation: dX/dt = F(t, X), where X(t) = (x_1, ..., x_n)^T and F = (f_1, ..., f_n)^T.",
      "An autonomous system satisfies dX/dt = F(X), where the vector field F does not explicitly depend on t.",
      "Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model: dy_1/dt = a y_1 - b y_1 y_2 and dy_2/dt = c y_1 y_2 - d y_2.",
      "Epidemic spread model: dN_i/dt = alpha N_i N_s - beta N_i and dN_s/dt = gamma(N_0 - N_s) - alpha N_s N_i."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 5,
    "title": "Linearity and Homogeneity Classifications",
    "scope": "Defines linearity and homogeneity for differential equations. Explains the structural definition of linear differential operators where the dependent variable and its derivatives appear to the first power with no product terms. Contrasts homogeneous systems with nonhomogeneous systems containing independent forcing terms, highlighting the role of the trivial solution.",
    "key_points": [
      "General linear ODE form: a_n(t) x^(n) + ... + a_1(t) x' + a_0(t) x = g(t), where coefficients depend exclusively on t.",
      "Nonlinear ODEs contain powers, products, or nonlinear functions of dependent variables (e.g., x^3 in Duffing, y_1 y_2 in Lotka-Volterra).",
      "A linear equation is homogeneous if g(t) = 0, admitting the trivial solution x(t) = 0.",
      "A linear equation is nonhomogeneous if g(t) != 0 (e.g., cooling equation dT/dt = -r T + r T_a due to constant r T_a, RLC with E(t) != 0).",
      "Lotka-Volterra is homogeneous in terms of external forcing despite its nonlinearity."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 6,
    "title": "Direction Fields and Tangent Slope Geometry",
    "scope": "Develops the geometric interpretation of first-order ODEs dx/dt = f(t, x) without analytical integration. Interprets f(t, x) as prescribing the tangent slope of solution trajectories across the coordinate plane. Details the step-by-step numerical and visual algorithm used to construct direction (slope) fields on discrete grids.",
    "key_points": [
      "The value f(t*, x*) directly prescribes the tangent slope k of the solution passing through (t*, x*).",
      "A direction field consists of line segments of fixed length L centered at grid points (t_i, x_j) with slope k_ij = f(t_i, x_j).",
      "Segment line equation: x - x_j = k_ij(t - t_i).",
      "Constraint on segment length: L must remain strictly smaller than grid spacings Delta t and Delta x to prevent crossing.",
      "Under existence and uniqueness conditions, exactly one smooth integral curve passes through each point tangent to the field."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 7,
    "title": "Qualitative Analysis via Direction Fields: Equilibria and Solution Families",
    "scope": "Examines how direction fields reveal global qualitative dynamics, integral curves, and steady states through three canonical prototypes. Analyzes parallel linear fields, asymptotic convergence to equilibrium in falling body problems, and radial fields. Concludes with a critical assessment of the strengths and limitations of slope fields.",
    "key_points": [
      "Constant right-hand side dx/dt = 1 produces an identical slope (k = 1) everywhere, generating parallel lines x(t) = t + C.",
      "Falling body model dv/dt = 9.8 - v/5 exhibits an equilibrium solution at dv/dt = 0 yielding steady-state terminal velocity v = 49 m/s.",
      "Qualitative stability: positive slopes below v = 49 m/s and negative slopes above drive all trajectories asymptotically toward 49 m/s.",
      "Homogeneous ratio dy/dx = y/x matches ray slopes from the origin, producing linear solution rays y = Cx.",
      "Advantages: no closed-form integration required, visual detection of equilibria, handles nonlinear equations.",
      "Limitations: purely qualitative, sensitive to grid resolution, computationally demanding manually, lacks point numerical values."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 8,
    "title": "The Method of Isoclines",
    "scope": "Presents isoclines as an efficient analytical-geometric method for constructing direction fields and sketching integral curves. Defines isoclines as loci of constant slope and provides the systematic multi-step workflow for curve tracing. Works through the concentric circle example dx/dt = sqrt(x^2 + t^2) and highlights the role of isoclines in qualitative ODE analysis.",
    "key_points": [
      "An isocline for dx/dt = f(t, x) is defined by the algebraic curve f(t, x) = C, along which all direction segments share the slope C.",
      "Workflow: select constants C_i, plot curves f(t, x) = C_i, draw uniform slope ticks of value C_i along them, and trace integral curves tangent to ticks.",
      "For dx/dt = sqrt(x^2 + t^2), isoclines are concentric circles x^2 + t^2 = C^2 centered at the origin with radius C (for C >= 0).",
      "Degenerate isocline C = 0 corresponds to the origin (0,0), where f(t, x) is non-differentiable.",
      "Integral curves cross circular isoclines with progressively steeper slopes (C = 1 gives 45 deg, C = 2 gives ~63 deg).",
      "Isoclines foster geometric intuition for identifying solution behavior, stability, and trajectory shapes prior to formal integration."
    ]
  }
]
